bread-ns-as-to-major-flour-toasted.title: Bread, NS as major flour, toasted

content.title: About
content.content: Bread made from major flour (NS) and toasted is a classic baked product with a crunchy crust and soft crumb. It is commonly used as a base for sandwiches, snacks, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Toasting enhances aroma through the Maillard reaction.
Bread from major flour (NS) has a more neutral taste than whole‑grain varieties.
Toasted bread has been served in ancient cultures together with olive oil and herbs.
A crisp crust forms at temperatures above 200 °C.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Bread provides a quick source of energy thanks to easily digestible carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Fermentation of the dough produces B1, B2 and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Toasting makes the bread easier to digest, and the crunchy crust stimulates saliva production.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Toasted bread can raise blood sugar quickly, which is relevant for people with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The product is unsuitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Some toasted breads contain added salt and preservatives; choose versions without unnecessary additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted bread works well for sandwiches, avocado toast, soup croutons, and as a base for appetizers. It can be spread with butter, nut pastes, or cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store toasted bread in a dry place in a paper bag or a ventilated container to keep the crust crisp. For longer storage, freeze it.

content.title: About
content.content: Goat meat is the meat of domestic goats, known as chevon (from mature goats) or cabrito (from kids). It is a lean, red meat with a flavor similar to lamb but milder and slightly sweeter, with less fat. Goat is widely eaten in South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, Latin America, and the Caribbean, and is used in curries, stews, roasts, and grills.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Goat is one of the most widely eaten red meats in many parts of the world.
Young goat is called cabrito or kid, and meat from mature goats is called chevon.
Goat meat is leaner than beef and lamb, so it benefits from slow, moist cooking.
It is a staple in curries and stews in South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and the Caribbean.
Goat has a milder flavor than mutton.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Goat meat provides complete protein for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Lower in fat than many red meats
items.content: Goat is leaner than beef and lamb and contains less saturated fat per serving.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Goat contains heme iron that the body absorbs readily.

items.title: Provides zinc and vitamin B12
items.content: These nutrients support immune function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked goat meat can carry harmful bacteria. Cook whole cuts to at least about 63 °C (145 °F) and let them rest, and ground goat to about 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Toughness when overcooked or cooked quickly
items.content: Because it is lean, goat meat can be tough and dry if cooked too fast or too long without moisture.

items.title: Red meat consumption
items.content: Health organizations generally suggest moderating red meat consumption.

items.title: Purines and cholesterol
items.content: Goat meat contains purines and cholesterol, which matters for people with gout or certain heart-related conditions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Goat meat is best cooked slowly with moisture, such as braised, stewed, or simmered in curries, soups, and pilafs, or marinated and grilled or roasted. Marinating in yogurt, lemon, or spices helps tenderize it. Serve it with vegetables and whole grains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw goat meat in the coldest part of the refrigerator and cook it within three to five days, or ground goat within one to two days. Freeze it for longer storage and thaw it in the refrigerator. Cooked goat should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days.

content.title: About
content.content: Mint Julep is a classic Southern United States cocktail made with bourbon, fresh mint, sugar and water. It is known for its refreshing flavor and aroma, usually served in a chilled julep cup with crushed ice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink originated in the early 19th century and became popular in Kentucky, especially in Lexington.
Traditionally it is served in a julep cup, which has a wide base and a narrow rim.
The original recipe uses a simple syrup (sugar + water), but many modern versions replace it with honey or agave.
Mint Julep is closely associated with the Kentucky Derby, where it is considered the official beverage of the event.
Mint leaves are often gently muddled before adding to the cocktail to release more aroma.

items.title: Contains mint
items.content: Mint is rich in menthol, which can aid digestion and provide a mild soothing effect.

items.title: Bourbon in moderation
items.content: Bourbon contains antioxidants such as polyphenols that may support cardiovascular health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Stress reduction
items.content: The scent of mint is often used in aromatherapy to reduce anxiety and improve mood.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Excessive alcohol consumption can lead to liver problems, dependence, and other health risks.

items.title: Sugar
items.content: Simple syrup adds calories and can contribute to tooth decay and blood sugar spikes.

items.title: Mint allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mint, resulting in skin rashes or swelling.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Serve Mint Julep in a chilled julep cup, gently muddle mint leaves, add bourbon, simple syrup, and top with cold water. Fill with crushed ice and garnish with a sprig of mint.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store alcoholic beverages in a cool, dark place. Keep simple syrup refrigerated in a sealed bottle for up to a month. Fresh mint should be stored in the refrigerator wrapped in a damp paper towel and used within a few days.

content.title: About
content.content: Onion (Allium cepa) is a biennial vegetable from the Amaryllidaceae family. When cooked with added fat (oil, butter, or animal fat) it becomes soft, mildly sweet, and golden‑brown. Cooked onions are a common base for sauces, stews, soups, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Onions contain sulfur compounds that turn into sweet sugars during heating, mellowing the flavor.
Caramelizing onions brings out a deep, slightly bitter aroma and a rich amber color.
Onions have been cultivated for over 5,000 years, making them one of the oldest vegetable crops.
In culinary practice onions are often called the "flavor foundation" because they underpin most dishes.
There are more than 600 onion varieties, differing in color, taste, and maturation time.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Onions provide quercetin and sulfur compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Sulfur compounds can help lower cholesterol levels and improve vascular tone.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of prebiotics
items.content: Fructans in onions feed beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Onions supply potassium, magnesium, and small amounts of iron.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to onions, ranging from mild itching to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Fructans can cause gas and bloating, especially in people with sensitive digestive systems.

items.title: High calorie content when fried
items.content: Adding large amounts of fat increases the dish’s calorie density, which should be considered in weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Sulfur compounds may enhance the effect of anticoagulants, so moderation is advised for those on blood thinners.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked onions with fat can be used as a base for sauces, gravies, stews, or as a side dish for meat, fish, or vegetables. They are also added to omelets, casseroles, and pizza. For a lighter taste, sauté in a small amount of oil until golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked onions in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions to preserve flavor and texture.

turkey-prepackaged-or-deli-luncheon-meat.title: Turkey, prepackaged deli, luncheon meat, reduced sodium (1015)

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey deli meat is a ready‑to‑eat sliced turkey product designed for sandwiches and snacks. The reduced‑sodium version (1015) contains about 1015 mg of sodium per 100 g, allowing lower salt intake without sacrificing flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is one of the leanest poultry meats, low in fat.
The slices are often smoked, giving a distinctive taste without a large amount of salt.
Sodium reduction is achieved by using salt substitutes and longer marination.
Reduced‑sodium turkey is popular in diet plans and sodium‑reduction programs.
The product is typically vacuum‑packed, extending shelf life.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Turkey contains less saturated fat than most red meats, supporting heart health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Provides about 20 g of complete protein per 100 g, essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: Lower salt content helps manage blood pressure and reduces kidney strain.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium supports immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey.

items.title: Preservative content
items.content: Certain versions may contain nitrites or other preservatives; check labels if you are sensitive.

items.title: Possible contamination
items.content: As a ready‑made product, improper storage can lead to microbial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use turkey slices in sandwiches, salads, wraps, or as a cold appetizer. Slice thinly for deli boards, melt briefly on hot sandwiches, or serve chilled with vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in the original packaging. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable curry is a fragrant dish made from a mix of vegetables, tomato base, coconut milk, and classic Indian spices such as turmeric, cumin, coriander and garam masala. It is rich in vitamins, minerals and plant protein, making it suitable for vegetarians and vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Curry originates from South Asian cuisine but now has countless regional variations.
Coconut milk softens the heat of the spices and gives the dish a creamy texture.
Vegetable curry can be adapted to seasonal produce: broccoli, cauliflower, bell pepper, carrot or pumpkin.
Traditionally it is served with basmati rice or naan flatbread.
The spices used in curry possess antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The vegetables and spices provide B6 and folate, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber from the vegetables aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Turmeric and coriander contain curcumin and other compounds that combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Cumin and paprika may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with a modest amount of oil or coconut milk, the dish remains heart‑friendly.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to turmeric, cumin or coriander.

items.title: Heat level
items.content: Excessive chili can cause stomach irritation in sensitive people.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain salt; monitor added salt to keep sodium intake moderate.

items.title: Coconut milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to coconut should substitute with another plant‑based milk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot vegetable curry with steamed rice, quinoa or whole‑grain flatbreads. Garnish with fresh cilantro, a squeeze of lime, or a dollop of yogurt for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked curry to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. Reheat on the stove or in a microwave, adding a splash of water or coconut milk to restore its creamy consistency.
